name: Jobs You Never Take: Hard Rules from Twelve Years at B-Tier
author: Old Bone (widely attributed to Terttu Jarvinen-Ekwueme)
description: A single-run zine, approximately 800 copies, photocopied on gray-market paper stock and distributed through Narrows drop points and at least two Shelf community boards in the 2190s. The document circulates as a personal set of operational rules from an experienced B-tier freelancer — not a guide in any formal sense, but a list of contract types the author refuses, and the reasoning behind each refusal. Tone is blunt, occasionally dark, and ends on a note that contradicts its own premise. Regularly cited in Signal Network forums as foundational reading for anyone trying to survive the transition from C to B-tier.
body:
JOBS YOU NEVER TAKE
Hard Rules from Twelve Years at B-Tier
— Old Bone

[printed on the cover: a hand-drawn bone with a question mark through it. below that, in smaller text: 'this is not advice. this is archaeology.']

---

I am not writing this to be wise. I am writing this because Pekko Rautiainen died in the Eastwall corridor seventeen months ago and nobody wrote anything about why, and I am tired of watching people I know make the same mistakes in the same order like there is a script for it. There is not a script. There is just a list of jobs you should not take, and most people learn it by dying partway through.

This is my list. It is not your list. You will add to it. The point is to have one.

---

**RULE ONE: Any job where you cannot independently verify the target's identity.**

The brief says: warehouse supervisor, mid-level logistics, no family presence at the site. You verify the name against two independent sources. Both confirm. You take the job.

Except both sources were fed by the same upstream node, and the name is a shell ident wrapped around a Tier 3 transport coordinator with three kids and a medical debt that has nothing to do with your client's interests. Someone made a mistake, or someone lied, and either way you are the mechanism.

Verification is not: the client tells you who it is. Verification is not: the drop includes a photo. Verification is: you have at least two sources that do not share a root, and at least one of them is physical — a face, a voice, a location you can confirm yourself before the job starts. If you cannot do this, the job does not exist for you yet. Go back to the client. If they push back on verification time, that is your answer.

This rule has no exceptions.

---

**RULE TWO: Any extraction job where you have not met the person being extracted.**

I know what the argument is. Sometimes you can't. The person is in a controlled environment, or the window is too short, or the client says contact would compromise the op. I have heard all of it.

Here is what I have also heard: 'extraction' used to mean 'removal by force of someone who does not want to be moved.' I have heard it mean 'we need a body delivered to a location and we don't want to explain why.' I have heard it mean 'the target thinks this is a rescue and it is not.'

You meet the person first. You hear from them, in person, unmonitored if possible, that they want to go. If the client cannot arrange that, you are not extracting a person. You are moving cargo. Decide if that is what you are.

---

**RULE THREE: Any sabotage brief that mentions 'no casualties' without specifying the enforcement mechanism.**

This sounds like a good line in a brief. 'Client requires zero civilian casualties.' Sounds like they care. Maybe they do.

Or: the brief was written to limit their legal exposure if something goes wrong. Or: 'no casualties' means 'no documented casualties.' Or: they want you to enforce a standard they have given you no tools to enforce, so that when it goes wrong, the liability is yours.

Ask: how is this enforced? What is the procedure if the timeline shifts and civilian presence increases? What are my abort conditions, and are they written into the contract? Who holds the breach if the brief's intelligence is wrong?

If they cannot answer these questions, 'no casualties' is decoration. It is a phrase on paper that protects them and does nothing for anyone else. Do not let it protect you from knowing what the job actually is.

---

**RULE FOUR: Jobs posted by anonymous clients offering above-market payout.**

The premium is not generosity. The premium is the price of whatever they cannot tell you.

Sometimes that is: the job is high-profile and they are paying for your silence. Fine. Sometimes it is: the job is illegal in a way that standard illegal is not. Sometimes it is: you are the third person to take this contract and the first two are somewhere in the Shelf right now wondering what happened.

Above-market pay means the market has already priced this correctly and the client disagrees. Find out why they disagree before you decide who is right.

Anonymous clients are not the problem by themselves. The Signal Network runs half its work through cutouts. But anonymous plus premium means two forms of non-transparency at once, and that is not a coincidence, it is a structure. Something is being hidden behind something else. Figure out what it is or leave the job alone.

Pekko took an anonymous premium job in the Eastwall corridor. I don't know all of it. I know the payout was listed at four times standard rate for a straightforward surveillance drop. I know the client was flagged anonymous-tier. I know Pekko needed the money because of the Northside thing the previous spring. I know he did not come back from that corridor. I know nobody posted a contract explanation after. That is what above-market anonymous looks like when you add it up.

---

**RULE FIVE: Any job that requires you to work with someone you cannot vouch for.**

This is the most argued rule in every conversation I have had about this list. People say: you can't always pick your team. You say: you are right, which is why sometimes you don't take the job.

A vouch is not a background check. It is not 'I have heard of them' or 'their Signal tier looks clean.' A vouch is: I have worked with this person, or someone I have personally worked with has worked with them and told me the specific truth of it. Not 'they're solid.' Solid means nothing. Solid means 'I like them' or 'they owe me a favor.'

What I need to know is: how do they behave when something goes wrong? How do they behave when there is an easier option that costs someone else? How do they behave when they are scared?

If I don't know those things through a chain I trust, I don't know them. And I do not work a job with someone I don't know. The job will go wrong in the exact way that tests the thing you don't know about them. It always does. That is not superstition, that is pattern recognition across twelve years.

---

That is the list. Five rules. I have kept four of them without exception.

The fifth one I broke three weeks ago.

The job came through a broker I trust, and the brief was clean, and the pay was standard, and the only problem was the partner: someone I had never worked with, vouched through a chain that had one link I couldn't personally verify. One link. The broker said the link was solid. I took that word for it.

I took the job. The job is done. Nobody died. It went fine.

I am still thinking about the one link I couldn't verify. I am thinking about it because it went fine, and because 'it went fine' is exactly what you think before the job that doesn't. I broke the rule and got the outcome I wanted and that is the most dangerous kind of lesson, because it teaches you that the rule is optional.

It is not optional. I broke it. I would like to not break it again.

The list stays the same.

— Old Bone

[bottom of last page, handwritten on the photocopy master before printing:]
*for Pekko. and for whoever finds this in a drop and reads it before they need it.*
